name: Shortfall — carrier commission recovery for small insurance agencies
one_liner: For the owner or office manager of a 5-50 person independent P&C insurance agency, Shortfall ingests the month's PDF/Excel carrier commission statements plus a policy-book CSV export and returns a ranked "money you are owed" list — policies missing from a statement, renewals paid at the wrong rate, chargebacks never reversed after reinstatement — with a ready-to-send carrier dispute email for each.
problem: Independent agencies are paid by 15-40 carriers, each sending direct-bill commission statements in its own PDF or Excel layout. Ivans DBCS automates this only for carriers that support it (an industry estimate puts ~40% of P&C carriers by volume outside ACORD 820 download), so the rest land as PDFs that a bookkeeper keys into Excel and eyeballs against the policy book. A published benchmark estimates 1.5-2 hours per carrier per month — 30-40 hours monthly at 20 carriers. Because the work is tedious, most agencies only tie out the statement total, not policy-level expected vs paid, so leakage survives: documented case studies show recoveries of $18,420 (outdated renewal rate, missing reinstatement credit, policies under an inactive producer code) and $31,400 across 2,840 policy lines. Catalyit's 2026 State of Tech Report says only 16% of agencies use any commission/billing/payment-management tool, so the other 84% are on spreadsheets or nothing. Producer splits are then calculated from those same spreadsheets, so an error becomes a payroll dispute too.
target_customer: Owner/principal or office manager of a 5-50 employee independent P&C agency (AMS: HawkSoft, EZLynx, NowCerts, QQ Catalyst, or QuickBooks only — i.e. the agencies Comulate and Applied do not chase). The buyer is the owner: it is their money, and they sign a $250-$600/month cheque without committee. Average US independent agency staff size is 9.9 (2026 Agency Universe Study), ~37,000 agencies.
why_now: Three things changed. (1) Multimodal models now parse arbitrary carrier PDF statement layouts reliably enough to do policy-level matching without per-carrier templates — a16z's 2026 Big Idea "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (Jennifer Li, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-1/) names exactly this bottleneck. (2) Cheap typed-decision models (TypeSafe's Jev, listed at $0.042/M input tokens on Cloudflare, https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai/models/typesafe/jev/ — the capability behind tonight's @shengkunye bookmark and YC's "Vertical Foundation Models" RFS) make the per-line match/no-match/why decision cost pennies for a 3,000-line month, which is what makes a $250-500/month price work on a small book. (3) The enterprise lane just got messier: the Jan 2026 Ardent (Comulate) v. Applied Systems complaint shows AMS data access for third parties is contested at the top of the market, which pushes a start-with-exports, no-AMS-integration product toward the small agencies nobody is fighting over. This also sits inside YC's "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (Brad Flora, https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#the-15-an-hour-expert): an agency CSR becomes the person who recovers commissions, no accountant needed.
comparables: Comulate (https://www.cbinsights.com/company/comulate) — commission reconciliation, $20M Series B (Feb 2025, BOND + Workday Ventures), customers are Lockton, Risk Strategies, IMA, Baldwin: explicitly large/PE-backed brokerages, enterprise contracts, and now entangled in litigation with Applied over Epic data access. Gap: nothing for a 12-person agency on HawkSoft. Ascend (https://www.useascend.com) — broad insurance finance stack (payments, premium finance, billing), one directory lists $750/user/month; reconciliation is a feature of a bigger platform, not a cheap point tool. Applied Epic / AMS360 native direct-bill reconciliation (https://www1.appliedsystems.com/en-us/platform/applied-epic/commission-reconciliation/) — only for agencies already on those systems (est. $150-300/user/month), and agencies still report resolving mismatches in Excel. Ivans DBCS (https://www.ivans.com/for-agents/products/ivans-download/) — automates the download where the carrier supports ACORD 820; an industry estimate says ~40% of P&C carriers by volume do not, and it delivers data, it does not tell you what you were underpaid. EZ Commissions ($250/month, https://www.capterra.com/p/10262304/EZ-Commissions/) and Policy Balance Hub (https://policybalancehub.com/) — closest direct competitors, both aimed at small agencies, both apparently founder-led with zero public reviews and no evidence of traction; EZ Commissions is a time-savings/processing tool, not a recovery tool. CommissionSight (https://commissionsight.com/pricing/) — priced "cents per member tracked", skews health/benefits. The open gap: small P&C agencies, no AMS integration required, and the output framed as recovered dollars rather than saved hours.
market_note: ~37,000 US independent agencies, average 9.9 staff (2026 Agency Universe Study). Estimate: 12,000-15,000 are in the 5-50 band with enough carriers to matter. At $350/month that is a $50-60M/year addressable line, before producer-payout and audit add-ons — enough for a real company, not a category-defining one, unless it expands into agency accounting. Willingness to pay is anchored by things buyers already spend on: offshore insurance BPO data entry at an indicative $6-16/agent-hour (so 30-40 hours/month ≈ $200-600 offshore, far more onshore), an in-house AP/bookkeeper role posted at ~$50-65k/year with commission reconciliation as a core duty, EZ Commissions listed at $250/month, Bind AI at $500-750/month, Outmarket Lite at $1,000/seat/year. All of these are vendor/third-party listed prices, not quotes I obtained. Leakage figures (3-7% of commissions, 15-25% of statements with an error) come from vendor marketing and should be treated as unverified claims; the two case-study recoveries ($18.4k, $31.4k) are single agencies.
risks: 1) The matching has to be right. A false "the carrier underpaid you" that the owner sends to their carrier rep is embarrassing and kills the account; the product must be ruthless about separating true underpayments from timing differences, legitimate chargebacks, endorsements and the agency's own stale policy data. 2) Small agencies are famously slow, low-ACV buyers with no procurement habit — 84% use no commission tool at all, which is as much evidence of apathy as of opportunity. CAC via conferences/FB groups could swamp a $350/month ticket. 3) Data acquisition: without AMS integration you depend on the owner exporting a policy CSV and dropping 20 PDFs each month. If that chore is not trivially easy, churn after month two is brutal. 4) Applied/Vertafore could ship "good enough" reconciliation downmarket, though their incentive is upmarket.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That policy-level matching from a messy PDF statement plus an imperfect policy-book CSV finds real, collectible money in a typical 10-person agency's first month — not just noise from timing and bad data. If the first run surfaces nothing recoverable, there is no sale. 2) That an owner will do the monthly chore of exporting the book and dropping statements, every month, without an AMS integration. 3) That the recoveries are large enough relative to $350/month that the owner renews — i.e. that the vendor-published 3-7% leakage claims hold at small-agency scale.
first_customers: Ten agencies with 8-30 staff, 15+ carriers, on HawkSoft/EZLynx/NowCerts/QQ Catalyst. Where to find them: the Catalyit user communities and solution-provider directory (catalyit.com), Big "I" state association chapters and their agency-management conferences, the r/InsuranceAgent and r/Insurance subreddits (existing threads on "horribly inefficient agency workflows" and duplicate entry across AMS/carrier portals), the Insurance Agency Owners and Agency Accounting Facebook groups, and HawkSoft's annual user group. Warmest entry: agency bookkeepers and AP specialists — search LinkedIn/Indeed for current "commission reconciliation specialist" postings at independent agencies and offer to run their last three months free.
validation_test: This week: find 5 agency owners/bookkeepers (Catalyit community, r/InsuranceAgent, Big "I" chapter, LinkedIn commission-reconciliation job posters) and offer a free "commission audit" — they send three months of statement PDFs for their five biggest carriers plus a policy-book CSV export, you run them by hand with an agent in a weekend and return a one-page list of suspected underpayments with dollar amounts. Pass: 3 of 5 send the files within a week, AND at least 2 of the 5 audits surface >$2,000 of plausible recoverable commission, AND at least 1 says "do this every month and I'll pay $350." Fail: they will not export the data, or the findings are all timing differences and their own data errors — which would mean the pain is hours, not money, and the whole pitch must flip back to time saved (a much harder sale at this price).
build_plan: Stack: TypeScript + Next.js, a frontier multimodal model (Claude/Gemini) for statement page → line-item extraction, a cheap typed-decision model (Jev-class) for the per-line match/exception classification, Postgres, no AMS integration in v1. Steps: (1) Build the statement parser: upload N PDFs/XLSX, output a normalised ledger (carrier, policy number, insured name, premium, commission paid, rate, period, transaction type). Hand-label 10 real statements from 10 carriers to get the extraction right — this is the whole moat in month one. (2) Build the book loader: accept HawkSoft/EZLynx/NowCerts/QQ policy exports and a generic CSV mapper. (3) Build the matcher: fuzzy match on policy number → insured name + effective date; compute expected commission from the agency's rate table (entered once per carrier/line of business); classify each exception as missing policy, rate variance, unreversed chargeback, producer-code error, or timing. (4) The one screen that matters: "You may be owed $X this month" with each line, the evidence, a confidence, and a one-click drafted carrier dispute email. (5) Producer-split report as the second screen — it is what turns a monthly audit into a monthly habit. Cut from v1: AMS write-back, payments, agency-bill AR, bank reconciliation, multi-user permissions, scanned/image-only statements (require text PDFs, OCR later), health/benefits lines.
launch_post: Every month your agency gets 20 carrier commission statements in 20 different PDF layouts, and someone ties out the totals in Excel. Shortfall reads them against your policy book and tells you which policies the carrier underpaid, missed, or charged back and never reversed. Free audit of your last 3 months.
reasoning:
Tonight's bookmarks are almost all AI-developer-tool material — a Claude skill demo, HackerTube, generated fonts, an agentic TPM, a cheap decision model, an outbound agent. Four of the obvious reads collapse straight into past ideas (Typecast, Canon, Exploded, Rightsline), so the useful signal was not the subjects but two capabilities: cheap typed per-item decisions at ~$0.002-$0.04 scale (@shengkunye's creator search, TypeSafe's Jev) and "an agent reads your messy inputs and finds the right targets" (Explee). Pointed at a buyer outside software, those become: read thousands of statement lines, decide per line whether the money is right, and surface only the ones worth a fight.

Shortfall beat the others because it is the only candidate where I could name the buyer (agency owner/principal, 5-50 staff), name what they pay today (a $50-65k/yr bookkeeper whose posted duties are literally commission reconciliation; offshore BPO at an indicative $6-16/agent-hour; EZ Commissions at $250/mo), show the incumbents pointing elsewhere (Comulate's customer list is Lockton and Risk Strategies, and 84% of agencies use no commission tool at all per Catalyit 2026), and describe a first version that a TypeScript builder can ship without an AMS integration or a licence. It is also squarely in this builder's lane: document in, structured decision out, agent as the edge — and unlike the surplus-lines and portal-fetch finalists there is no regulatory liability or credential-handling risk gating the first sale.

Where I stayed honest: the headline leakage percentages are vendor marketing, the two recovery case studies are single agencies, and the small-agency buyer is notoriously slow. The validation test is built to kill it fast — if three free audits surface nothing but timing differences, the recovery framing dies and the idea reverts to a hours-saved pitch that will not carry $350/month. It builds on nothing in the library; the nearest neighbours (Stalecheck, Dockproof) share the "reconcile against an external source of truth" shape but serve AP managers and retail ops, not agency owners, and do not touch commission data.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Shortfall — carrier commission recovery for small P&C agencies (PICK). Named buyer with budget, recurring monthly pain, documented recoveries, incumbents visibly aimed upmarket.
2. Outbound compliance/audit layer for AI SDR agencies (from the Explee bookmark) — dropped at screen: CAN-SPAM/GDPR content is commodity blog material, no named buyer with a budget line, and deliverability monitoring is already bundled into Instantly/Smartlead/Mailforge.
3. Deliverability reputation watchdog for multi-client outbound agencies — dropped at screen: Google Postmaster + Microsoft SNDS are free and Mission Inbox/Mailforge already sell this exact workflow to this exact buyer.
4. "Agentic TPM" for non-software programs (construction, clinical trials) off the Serro bookmark — dropped at screen: Serro itself plus every PM incumbent is converging here, and the non-software version needs a long enterprise sale far from a weekend-capable wedge.
5. Jev-powered ticket/claims triage router sold to insurance TPAs — dropped at screen: it is a model capability, not a product; the buyer and the workflow stayed vague and it collides with every AI-ops vendor.
6. Creator-rights/whitelisting ops from the UGC-discovery bookmark — DROPPED AS A REPEAT of Rightsline (2026-10-30), same buyer, same core workflow.
7. HN-comment-style public-dataset curation product (Karpathy/HackerTube) — DROPPED AS A REPEAT of Canon (2026-11-01) and Hiringscope; also a build, not a venture.
8. Generative-font / exploded-diagram productisation (elvar + nutlope bookmarks) — DROPPED AS REPEATS of Typecast (2026-11-02) and Exploded (2026-10-26).
9. Surplus-lines tax filing automation for wholesale brokers (non-software buyer, regulatory deadlines) — FINALIST, lost: InsCipher already runs a managed 50-state filing service with software, the per-state rule corpus is a heavy moat to build before first revenue, and penalty exposure makes a solo-built v1 risky. Worth revisiting.
10. Carrier-portal fetch agent for agencies (login to 20+ portals, pull docs/statements) — FINALIST, lost: real pain (67% of agents use 5+ carrier portals weekly; 37% cite multiple logins as friction) but Access My Insurance and Carrier Connect AI already sell it, and MFA/credential-storage/ToS risk is a nasty first product for a solo builder. Its best piece — getting the statements — folds into Shortfall later.
11. "$15-an-hour expert" back-office pod for independent agencies (AI-backed CSR doing certificates and renewals) — dropped at screen: it is a services business, not a product; competes with established insurance BPOs on price.

PROJECT
1. Regretcheck — drop package.json, get what HN says about every dependency with migration quotes and a regret score. PICK. Personal input, public data nobody has pointed at a manifest, free data layer, a return loop.
2. Canon-style HN video shelf — dropped immediately as a repeat of the past idea Canon (same HackerTube data, same tick-the-canon workflow).
3. Font generator from a URL — dropped immediately as a repeat of Typecast (nutlope font post, same core workflow).
4. Teardown-in-the-browser: paste a gadget name, get an interactive exploded "how it works" page — finalist, LOST. Deep research found teardownai.app already does photo→exploded view (paid, $4.99/10 scans), Computer's Teardown skill is free until 6 Nov, and the past idea Exploded covers photo→exploded diagram. Repeat risk plus crowded in the same week elvar's skill trended.
5. Repo→animated "how it works" explainer page — dropped at screen. GitDiagram already does repo→interactive diagram + narrated explainer video free (gitdiagram.com), and several Claude skills (dynamic-archify, architecture-diagram-skill, ai-archi) generate single-file animated HTML. Well-known free version exists.
6. HackerShelf-style books shelf from the HackerBooks CSV — dropped at screen. hackerbooks.org shipped 2 Nov with 16,543 books and a downloadable CSV; HackerShelf exists too. The shelf presentation is taken.
7. "What should I read next" — Goodreads CSV × HN book mentions — finalist, LOST. Data checked and clean (Goodreads has a real CSV export; Open Library covers are hotlinkable at 100 req/5min per IP), and no tool combines the two. But it is one-time (you import once, get a list, leave), the audience overlaps the Canon past idea, and the output card is a reading list, which is a weaker post than a verdict on your stack.
8. Startup follower-growth tracker from @benln's chart — dropped at screen. Requires paid X API access for follower history, no free data path, and Social Blade-style tools already cover the ground.
9. Creator-discovery card built on the typesafe/Jev UGC endpoint — dropped at screen. Jev is real and cheap ($0.042/M input at model pricing) but the underlying creator data is the product, it is someone else's launch from the bookmarks, and the output ("here are small creators") is not personal or postable.
10. Kindle My Clippings.txt → "your reading year" card — dropped at screen. Parsing is easy and browser-local, but the file is partial (only books with highlights), the output is a Spotify-Wrapped clone, and nothing recent makes it newly possible.
11. Jev-powered "is this HN comment praise or a migration story" classifier demo — dropped at generate; it is infrastructure, not a product anyone opens twice. Its useful half was absorbed into Regretcheck's classification pass.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised Explee (outbound agent, $0.04/email, no subscription), Serro AI (agentic TPM — confirmed it is already the thing, so cloning it was out), and TypeSafe's Jev (typed decisions, $0.042/M input tokens on Cloudflare) — the Jev read is what made the cheap-per-line-decision economics in Shortfall credible. A fourth call on the Alfred Lin article (Kalshi Series A deck) was spent from reading and returned nothing usable; the Dwarkesh/Caro and follower-growth bookmarks were skipped as noise.

Screening pot (6/6): checked cold-email deliverability tooling (killed candidates 2 and 3 — Mission Inbox, Mailforge, Instantly already own it), city permit AI (returned nothing, and the permit lane is adjacent to Backcheck anyway), UGC whitelisting (confirmed as a Rightsline repeat), Jev use cases (confirmed it is a capability not a product), AI-SDR compliance (no buyer with a budget line), and commercial insurance submission intake (surfaced Convr, CoverForce, InEvo, Outmarket — told me the submission lane is crowded and pushed me to the back-office/money lane instead).

Deep research pot (12/12): mapped the insurance-agency back office. Found Comulate's $20M Series B and enterprise customer list, Ascend, Bind AI ($500-750/mo) and Outmarket Lite ($1,000/seat/yr); AMS pricing (HawkSoft $99/concurrent user, Epic ~$150, AMS360 $150-300); the Ivans DBCS coverage estimate (130+ carriers on ACORD 820, ~40% of P&C carriers by volume outside it); the 1.5-2 hrs per carrier per month benchmark; Catalyit's 16% adoption figure; the $18,420 and $31,400 recovery case studies; BPO rates of $6-16/agent-hour offshore; current job postings for commission reconciliation specialists at $50-65k; and the Ardent v. Applied complaint plus Applied's API terms, which is what convinced me v1 must not depend on AMS integration. This pot moved the idea from "submission intake" to "commission recovery" and from "any agency" to "agencies not on Epic/AMS360".

Sharpening pot (5/5, 2 rounds): verified that products aimed at the small end exist but are thin (EZ Commissions $250/mo with zero Capterra reviews, Policy Balance Hub unverifiable ownership, both PDF+CSV with no AMS requirement — which both proves the workflow is buildable and leaves the gap open); verified producer-split calculation is done in spreadsheets off the same data (second screen of the product); and tried and failed to verify any contingency-fee commission-recovery vendor or any independent leakage benchmark — so pain stayed at 8 rather than 9 and the contingency pricing model was dropped from the plan.

Investor signals weighed: a16z's "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (Jennifer Li) is the direct enabler and is cited in why_now; YC's "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (Brad Flora) frames the buyer outcome; YC's "Vertical Foundation Models" (Diana Hu) supports the cheap typed-decision layer. I deliberately did not pursue "AI for City Hall" (too close to Backcheck) or the space/data-centre signals (no bookmark gave a way in and no fit with this builder).
Sharpening (7.1 to 7.9): Round 1 — weak criterion: gap (6.5). The first shape of the idea was "AI commission reconciliation for insurance agencies", which runs straight into Comulate ($20M Series B, BOND/Workday), Ascend, and native Applied Epic/AMS360 reconciliation. Change: narrow the buyer to 5-50 person agencies NOT on Epic/AMS360 (HawkSoft, EZLynx, NowCerts, QQ Catalyst, QuickBooks-only) and require no AMS integration — statements plus a CSV export only. Research: Comulate's own named customers are Lockton, Risk Strategies, IMA, Baldwin — explicitly large/PE-backed brokerages (cbinsights/teardown), and the Jan 2026 Ardent v. Applied complaint shows AMS data access is a contested dependency at that tier, which argues for staying off integrations in v1. Only two products visibly serve the small end — EZ Commissions ($250/mo) and Policy Balance Hub — both with zero public reviews and no evidence of traction, and Catalyit's 2026 report puts commission/billing/payment tool adoption at 16%. Gap 6.5 → 8.

Round 2 — weak criteria: pain (7) and wedge (7). The product was framed as "save your bookkeeper 30 hours a month", which is a cost-saving sale to a buyer with cheap labour (offshore BPO at an indicative $6-16/agent-hour makes hours look affordable). Change: reframe the first version as a recovery product — the output is "you may be owed $14,870 this month", with per-line evidence and a drafted carrier dispute email, and producer-split impact as the second screen. Research: documented case studies of $18,420 and $31,400 recovered from exactly the error classes a matcher can detect (outdated renewal rate, unreversed reinstatement chargeback, inactive producer code, missing policies); a published benchmark of 1.5-2 hrs per carrier per month supports the hours too. Caveat found and kept honest: the 3-7% leakage and 15-25% error-rate figures are vendor marketing, not independent research, and no established contingency-recovery vendor with a published fee could be verified — so I did not raise pain to 9. Pain 7 → 8, wedge 7 → 8. Timing held at 7.5: the multimodal-parsing and cheap-typed-decision enablers are real and recent, but I did not find a dated deadline forcing agencies to act.

Project: READING POT (3/3 used). (1) Perplexity on the HackerTube zip: established the export is 17.8 MB, 6,454 videos, 39,834 labelled comments, ODC-By licensed — which told me the HackerTube data itself is already fully mined and pushed me off any direct derivative (and it would have repeated the past idea Canon). (2) Perplexity on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on Together: $0.30/M in, $1.20/M out, 1M context, released 17 Oct 2026 — confirmed the cheap-classification building block but also showed font/SVG generation is just code generation, killing any font angle (also a repeat of Typecast). (3) Perplexity on elvar's Claude skill: it is "teardown", MIT, Claude-Code-only, produces offline HTML 3D simulators — told me the teardown space was a skill, not a web app, which kept candidate #4 alive into screening.

SCREENING POT (5/5 used). One search each on: startup follower-growth trackers (no free data path, Social Blade covers it → dropped); YouTube chapter/summary tools (saturated, dozens of free ones → dropped a video-tooling angle); the teardown skill's prior art (found teardownai.app and whatpeoplemade.com, flagged crowding); Jev/typesafe pricing (real, $0.042/M input, but infrastructure not product); HackerBooks (shipped 2 Nov with a CSV → killed the books-shelf candidate outright). Net effect: four of ten candidates died before deep research, and the HN-derivative wave became visible as a pattern rather than one post.

DEEP RESEARCH POT (8/8 used). Spent on the three finalists. For Regretcheck: confirmed HackerChurn exists and what exactly it does (SaaS tools, ≥3 complaints across 2 threads, nightly refresh, part of HissingKitty) — this both validated the hook and defined the gap, since it covers no libraries and takes no user input; confirmed BigQuery's bigquery-public-data.hacker_news holds the full archive free under 1 TiB/month; confirmed HN Algolia is free, keyless, CORS-enabled, 10k req/hour/IP and fine for ~50 parallel lookups from a static page; ran a targeted prior-art check for manifest→HN-sentiment tools and found only adjacent things (Safeguard = CVEs, Revenant = abandonment signals from project health, neither uses human comments). For the books finalist: confirmed Goodreads has a real CSV export and Kindle My Clippings.txt is partial, and that Open Library covers are hotlinkable but capped at 100 req/5min — buildable, but the research also surfaced HackerShelf, weakening novelty. For teardown: confirmed teardownai.app charges and the free alternatives are Claude skills, which plus the Exploded repeat retired it. Also checked whatpeoplemade.com for a dataset (none public) and Together's batch API (50k requests/file, up to 50% off) which set the ~$20 cost estimate for the classification pass.

SHARPENING POT (4/4 used). Two rounds, two calls each, documented in sharpen_notes: round 1 verified the weekly-refresh data path was free and that HackerChurn already refreshes nightly (usefulness 5→6); round 2 verified no repo/manifest share-card prior art beyond GitDiagram's MP4 export and that HackerBooks/HackerChurn both hit the HN front page this week (shareability 6→8, wow 7→8). Score moved 7.2 → 7.4 → 8.0. What did NOT change: usefulness stayed at 6 because no evidence showed weekly sentiment drift is real, and freshness stayed at 9 rather than 10 because the enabling pieces (the model, the HN wave) are days-to-weeks old, not released today.
Sharpening (7.4 to 8): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (5 before: a one-time toy; you check your stack once and never return). Change to the idea: added "watch this stack" — the manifest is stored in localStorage and re-scored weekly against the refreshed dataset, surfacing two specific events, a package whose regret score moved and a package where the FIRST migration story just appeared. Research: confirmed the data layer supports a weekly refresh cheaply — HN Algolia is free, keyless, CORS-enabled at 10k req/hour/IP (https://hn.algolia.com/api, https://cors.dev/guides/hacker-news-api) and the BigQuery HN public dataset is free under the 1 TiB/month allowance, so a nightly/weekly re-pull costs nothing; HackerChurn already refreshes its HN-derived data nightly, which proves the refresh cadence is practical. Usefulness 5 → 6, not higher: I could not verify that package sentiment actually moves week to week, so the return loop is plausible but unproven. Score 7.2 → 7.4.

Round 2 — weak criterion: shareability (6 before: a table of your own dependencies is interesting to you and boring to everyone else). Change: added the Regret Report card — a single number for your whole stack, plus "HN would most like you to drop: X" and "HN would defend: Y", built as a posted image rather than a link. Research: checked prior art for repo-to-share-card tools and found GitDiagram exports landscape/vertical MP4s of repo architecture (https://gitdiagram.com/) but nothing producing a sentiment/opinion card from a manifest; separately confirmed the format's pull — HackerBooks and HackerChurn both reached the HN front page within days of HackerTube using the same "HN comments as a product" hook (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50326821, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50353386). Shareability 6 → 8: the output is now a card built to be posted, and near-identical formats demonstrably spread this week. Wow 7 → 8 on the same change (one dropped file returns a verdict on your whole stack, which is not what people expect). Score 7.4 → 8.0.
prototype_summary: Shortfall prototype: eight messy carrier commission statements run through a simulated reconciliation into a ranked, evidence-backed list of 11 items worth $14,870 the agency is owed, with dispute-email drafting and producer payout impact.
